t: after midday. From the midpoint of the day onward (see below, halachah 4).
from the sheep or from the goats... a year old. A lamb or kid within its first year.

and both men and women are obligated in this commandment. Although the Paschal offering is a time-bound positive commandment, from which women are generally exempt, here women are obligated (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3). This is learned from the verse "according to the number of persons" (Exodus 12:4), which includes women (Mekhilta, Bo, Pischa, section 3).
and he is not impure and not on a distant journey. For those who are impure or far away are exempt from the Paschal offering and are deferred to the Second Pesach (below, chapter 5).

and if he neglected it unintentionally, he is exempt. From a sin offering. Although for every negative commandment whose deliberate violation carries karet, one who violates it unintentionally is liable for a sin offering, with the Paschal offering the law differs because this is a positive commandment (see Hilchot Shegagot 1:2).

only in the Temple court, like the other sacrificial offerings. Like all offerings of lesser sanctity, which are slaughtered anywhere in the Temple court (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:4), and not outside it.

at the time when private altars were permitted. Before the Tabernacle was erected in the wilderness, and from entering the Land until the Tabernacle was set up at Shiloh, and from the destruction of Shiloh until the building of the Temple in Jerusalem; during all those times it was permitted to offer sacrifices on private altars outside the Temple (Mishnah, Zevachim 14:4-8).
on a private altar. A raised structure serving as an altar, which a private person set aside for offering (for example, on the top of his roof and the like; see Tosefta, Zevachim 13:15).

on a public altar. The altar before the Tent of Meeting after entering the Land of Israel, as it was at Nob and Gibeon before the Temple was built in Jerusalem; this altar had laws similar to the altar in the Temple (see Mishnah, Zevachim 14:10).
as if he had offered it in the marketplace. In a place with no sanctity at all.
they learned from tradition. The Sages' tradition of interpreting the verses.
the slaughter of the Paschal offering is after midday. For it says of it "between the evenings" (Exodus 12:6), that is, from the time the sun begins to decline toward the west, which is after midday.
after the daily offering of the afternoon. No offering is slaughtered after the afternoon daily offering, except the Paschal offering alone (see Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 1:3-4).
after they burn the afternoon incense and after they tend the lamps. For these are the last two services in the order of the daily offering (ibid. 6:4).

and one person stirs the blood of the Paschal offering until the blood of the daily offering is sprinkled. They stir the blood until after the daily offering's blood is sprinkled so that it does not congeal.
in its time. On the fourteenth of Nisan after midday.
an olive-bulk of chametz in his possession. He owned chametz in the amount of an olive-bulk, which is the amount for which one is liable to karet for eating on Pesach (Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 1:1).
in the possession of one of them. Of those performing the services of the offering.
one of the members of the group that eats this Paschal offering. For the Paschal offering is eaten in groups of people, the chavurot (below 2:1).
he receives lashes. The one performing the service of the offering.
and the Paschal offering is valid. It was not disqualified by the transgression.
requires pouring against the base. That he stands near the altar at one of the three corners under which there is a base, and pours the blood directly onto the base (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:17).
they flay it. Remove the skin.
its fats. The fats and other parts of the offering that are offered on the altar (for their enumeration see there 1:18).

the fats of each sacrifice separately. They are careful that it not be mixed with the fats of the other Paschal offerings, and the same applies to other offerings (ibid. 10:16); therefore they put the fats of each Paschal offering in its own vessel (below, halachah 14).
and goes out to his home in Jerusalem. For it is permitted to eat the Paschal offering anywhere in the city, as with offerings of lesser sanctity (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:5).
and roasts it. For the only permitted way to cook the Paschal offering is roasting (below, chapter 8).
and eats it at night. On the night of the Seder.

one who leaves the fats and does not burn them until they stayed overnight and were disqualified by remaining overnight. That he left them the entire night until morning, and they are disqualified by this.

he does not receive lashes because there is no act in it. Because he committed a transgression without performing an actual act, and one does not receive lashes for a transgression unless it involves an act (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).

until dawn rises. The beginning of daylight, which is the end of the night. However, to keep far from negligence, the Sages enacted that they be burned until midnight (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:2).
when the fourteenth falls on Shabbat etc.. In such a case it is permitted to offer the fats on the night of the festival (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 1:7-8).
the fats of a weekday sacrifice are not burned on a festival. The burning of the fats is not deferred to a sanctified day, but its fats must be burned on that same day.
in three groups. Those offering divide into three groups, and each group slaughters the Paschal offerings by itself.
if there were fifty in all. There were only fifty people who brought the offerings, and they want to divide into three groups of thirty.
and ten go out and ten come in. And in this way they count as a different group.
and if all slaughtered at once. In one group.
and they lock the doors of the Temple court. So that others will not crowd in to enter.
repeat. Recite a second time.
recite a third time. Recite a third time.
and they never completed a third time. Because the work of offering was done with great speed, there was no need for a third recitation.
for each and every recitation etc.. Before each time they begin reciting Hallel.

since it has no libations, to sound the trumpets at the time of the libation. For with the daily offering, the priests sounded the trumpets and blasts and the Levites sang at the time of the wine libation (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 6:5-7), but the Paschal offering has no libations.
the priests stand in rows. Each row extends from the place of slaughter to the altar.
and in their hands are silver basins and gold basins. Vessels for receiving the blood and carrying it to the altar.
and the basins had no bases. The basin had no flat bottom on which it could be stood, but a pointed bottom.

he gives it to his fellow and his fellow to his fellow, so that many will be engaged in the commandments. Each passes the basin to the priest standing next to him in the row, and they do not give it to one priest to carry the blood to the altar alone, in order to increase those engaged in the commandment.
he pours it in one pouring against the base. For this is the commandment for applying the blood of Paschal offerings (above, halachah 6).
and clears out its innards etc.. Cleans the intestines and removes the waste from them.
and salts them. Sprinkles salt on them, as with anything burned on the altar, which must be salted (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
iron nails were fixed in the walls and pillars. A sort of hooks that were hung on the walls of the Temple court.
sticks. Poles.
they wash the Temple court. Of the blood and dirt that accumulated on the floor.
even with something that is not needed for the service. For rinsing the floor is not among the needs of the service but is for cleanliness.
it is permitted. Permitted even at the outset.
as its procedure on a weekday, so its procedure on Shabbat. On Shabbat they slaughter the Paschal offerings in exactly the same way as they would on a weekday.

and they wash the Temple court on Shabbat, for there is no shevut prohibition in the Temple. Rinsing the floor is forbidden on Shabbat as a shevut and is not a full labor prohibited by the Torah (see Hilchot Shabbat 21:3)
,. therefore they permitted doing it in the Temple.
each person does not carry his Paschal offering to his home on Shabbat. For on Shabbat it is forbidden to carry things from a private domain to a public domain (Hilchot Shabbat 12:8).
on the Temple Mount. Which is surrounded by a wall (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:1), and all of it together with the Temple is one domain.
in the chel. The area enclosed by a partition between the wall of the Temple Mount and the Temple court (ibid. 5:3).
with his Paschal offering. He takes the offering with him.
they override Shabbat. Although performing them involves full labors, it is permitted to do them if the fourteenth of Nisan falls on Shabbat.
riding it. Carrying the animal on the shoulder to bring it to the Temple (see Hilchot Shabbat 18:16).
and bringing it from outside the boundary. Beyond the distance one may walk on Shabbat (see ibid. 27:1).

and cutting its wart with an implement etc.. Which is an act of repair and forbidden on Shabbat. They permitted doing it without an implement, which is an unusual manner, or when the wart is dry, in which case the repair is not significant (see ibid. 9:8).
he should not bring it on Shabbat. For he transfers it from one domain to another.
but he may place it between the horns of the lamb etc.. He tucks it in so that it does not fall off the body of the sacrificial animal, and the animal carries the knife to the Temple, not the person.
and strikes it. Hits the animal to drive it so that it walks.
and consecrates it there. For the reason explained shortly.
even though he is loading on Shabbat. He places a load on the animal, which is forbidden on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 20:1).
he loads in an unusual manner. Not in the ordinary manner of the labor, since these animals do not ordinarily carry loads (Rashi, Pesachim 66b).
because he is working with consecrated animals. And it is forbidden to do any work with them (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:7).
and why did they permit consecrating one's Paschal offering on Shabbat. For ordinarily it is forbidden to consecrate on Shabbat and festivals (Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).
since its time is fixed etc.. For it is the commandment of the day (ibid.).
and it was found to be blemished or a treifah. And it was discovered that the offering is invalid.

or until it becomes dark and he is deferred to the Second Pesach etc.. For once the night of the fifteenth arrives, the Paschal offering cannot be slaughtered, and if he does not find a valid animal he is deferred to the Second Pesach.
for he is prevented by circumstances beyond his control. He was prevented from bringing the Paschal offering through no fault of his own.
only for those counted for it. Only for those who joined beforehand with the people eating that same offering.

as it says, "you shall be counted for the lamb". The word "takhosu" is interpreted as an expression of counting, as at the beginning of the same verse: "he and his neighbor next to his house shall take according to the number of persons" (and see Targum Onkelos).
while it is alive. That one must be counted for it before the slaughter (below, halachah 14), while it is still called a "lamb" and not a "sacrifice."
and an individual who slaughtered the Paschal offering for himself. When he is alone, without a group.
provided that he is able to eat all of it. That he is capable of eating it alone.
as it says, "they shall make it". In the plural, meaning in a group of people, since it is preferable to slaughter for many (Birkat Avraham, sec. 5).
if he can eat an olive-bulk, one may slaughter for him. It is permitted to slaughter for him among the other members of the group, since eating an olive-bulk is considered eating.

even a group of a hundred, none of whom can eat an olive-bulk etc.. Although together they could eat the entire lamb, one does not slaughter for them, since eating less than an olive-bulk does not count.
because of the levity that would be among them. For they might come to immodesty together.

they may make a group entirely of women, even for the Second Pesach. Women may form a group by themselves to offer the Second Pesach, although they are not obligated in the Second Pesach but it is optional for them (as below 5:8).
and they slaughter for minors to be among the members of the group. That they join a group that includes adults.

not that a group be entirely minors who lack understanding. For they might thereby disqualify the Paschal offering (Aruch HaShulchan 184:15; similarly Likutei Halachot, Pesachim 91b). Some explained that one does not slaughter for them by themselves because they are not obligated (Meiri, Pesachim 91a).

entirely sick people or elderly or onanim. An onen is one whose relative died that day, and because of the grief he may not eat much (for the details of the law of an onen eating the Paschal offering see below 6:9).
lest they leave over some of the Paschal offering and bring it to disqualification. That they will not manage to eat all of it, and the meat will become leftover and invalid.

lest they be overly particular about it and bring it to disqualification. Because they are not well versed in the laws of the Paschal offering, they might be stringent and disqualify it without justification.
he slaughtered it not for those counted for it. For people who were not counted for it.
for one none of whom can eat an olive-bulk. That there is not even one in the entire group who can eat an olive-bulk.
for the uncircumcised or the impure. Who are forbidden to eat of the Paschal offering (below, chapter 5).
he slaughtered it for one who can eat and for one who cannot eat etc.. He had in mind both the qualified and the disqualified together.

and sprinkled the blood for the circumcised and the uncircumcised, it is invalid, for the sprinkling is more severe, being the essence of the offering. Therefore a thought regarding the circumcised and uncircumcised disqualifies it (unlike slaughter, which is valid with such a thought).
he slaughtered it for the circumcised so that the uncircumcised would be atoned through it. At the time of slaughter he intended that the blood be sprinkled on behalf of the uncircumcised.

for there is a thought of the uncircumcised in the sprinkling. A thought that disqualifies in the sprinkling disqualifies even if he thought of the sprinkling at the time of slaughter (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:10).

he slaughtered it for those who can eat, to sprinkle its blood for those who cannot eat. He slaughtered for the sake of those able to eat an olive-bulk of it, and at the time of slaughter he intended to sprinkle the blood for those unable to eat an olive-bulk.

the Paschal offering is valid but a person does not fulfill his obligation with it. The offering is not disqualified, and it is permitted to sprinkle its blood and burn its fats, but one does not fulfill the obligation of the Paschal offering with it, and they need a new offering or are deferred to the Second Pesach.

because a thought of eaters does not apply to the sprinkling. For had he thought at the time of sprinkling the blood itself that it was for those unable to eat, the offering would not have been disqualified, but it could not be eaten since the blood was sprinkled not for its eaters. Therefore, even if he had this thought at the time of slaughter, the offering is not disqualified and one does not fulfill the obligation with it.
one who is healthy at the time of slaughter and sick at the time of sprinkling. And at that time he is unable to eat an olive-bulk.
a person slaughters through his minor son and daughter etc.. He appoints them to the Paschal offering even against their will, for they are under his authority (see below, halachah 9).
but he does not slaughter through his adult son and daughter... except with their consent. With their agreement, for they are in their own domain.
and if they were silent and did not object, it is with their consent. For presumably they want to be counted for his Paschal offering.
and they went and slaughtered for themselves. With another group, and did not want to be counted with their father or master.
they fulfill their obligation with their master's. For he slaughters for them without their consent.

and they slaughtered for themselves, there is no greater protest than this. For it is clear from their actions that they do not want what he slaughtered for them, even though they said nothing explicitly.
she eats from her husband's. For presumably her place is there.
she was hurrying to go to her father's house. Hurrying to go there for the festival.
she eats from her father's. For presumably she prefers it there.
from then on. If she goes to her father's house after the first festival following marriage.

provided that she chooses a place she wants at the time of slaughter. She must decide beforehand whether she is counted for her husband's or her father's Paschal offering, for the identity of those counted is fixed until the time of slaughter (below, halachah 14).
an orphan for whom guardians slaughtered etc.. The adults responsible for him and his property, for example where two guardians each slaughtered a Paschal offering for him.
he eats from the place he wishes. He may decide where to eat even after the slaughter, since a minor is counted for the Paschal offering without his consent (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
with a minor orphan. For one slaughters for a minor without his consent (above, halachah 8).
he is as one who counts himself for two Paschal offerings. Whereas in practice there is no such possibility.
he eats only from the one slaughtered first. Which was slaughtered validly for him.
when they are particular about one another. That they do not yield, and neither wants the other to benefit from his property (Rabbeinu Chananel, Pesachim 88a).
he may not eat from either of them. He is forbidden to eat from either one.
one who is half slave and half free. He belonged to two partners, and one freed him.
he may not eat etc.. For this status is temporary, and the master is obligated to free him (see Hilchot Avadim 7:7).
up to how many are counted for the Paschal offering. What is the largest number of people fit to be counted for one Paschal offering.
an olive-bulk for each and every one. An olive-bulk of the meat of the Paschal offering for each of those counted.
and they withdraw their hands from it. They cancel their partnership in it.
once it is slaughtered, he cannot withdraw his hand etc.. From the time of slaughter onward, it is not possible to cancel the partnership, and he is counted among those counted for that offering.
the first ones who have an olive-bulk. Who were counted when there was still an olive-bulk of meat in the lamb for each of them.
do not eat and are obligated to observe the Second Pesach. For they are not considered counted at all, and this Paschal offering was not offered for them.
one who counts others with him for his portion etc.. He added more people to be counted for the portion due to him, without receiving permission from the rest of the group.
the members of the group may give him a portion etc.. The rest of the group can say they do not wish others to eat with them and reduce their portion.
and likewise members of a group one of whom was a glutton. A big eater, and they do not want him to overeat at the expense of their portions.
to remove him from among them, and they give him his portion and he eats it with his own group. That he receive the portion due him and eat separately from them.
and if he is not a glutton, they may not split off. Without agreement (Meiri, Pesachim 89b).
even though his master's practice is to slaughter a lamb every year. Even if the master always slaughters a lamb (from the sheep) for the Paschal offering.
and he went and slaughtered a kid for him. The slave departed from the custom and slaughtered a kid (from the goats).

for he did not specify etc.. Since the master did not say explicitly which kind he wanted slaughtered, and said simply "a Paschal offering," his instruction covers all possibilities, and what the slave did is valid.
he went and slaughtered a kid and a lamb. If the slave slaughtered both kinds because of the uncertainty.

but they go out to the place of burning, since one is not counted for two Paschal offerings. Both Paschal offerings are invalid, because it is not possible to be counted for two animals and clarify afterward which of them will be eaten.

and if it was a king or queen... he eats from the first, for the sake of the peace of the kingdom. Because of fear of the rulers' anger, they permitted this (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon, and see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 8:2).
and he designated for him a kid or a lamb. He told him explicitly which kind to bring.
he slaughters a kid and a lamb. He brings one of each kind, one for the one who sent him and the other for himself.
and he says: if a kid, he told me a kid is his and the lamb is mine etc.. After the slaughter he asks the sender what he told him, gives him that one, and the agent takes the other for himself.
both go out to the place of burning. Both Paschal offerings are burned.
before the blood is sprinkled, they are obligated to observe the Second Pesach. For at the time of its offering it was not fit for eating, and it is invalid.
after the blood is sprinkled, they are exempt from observing the Second Pesach. For the offering was slaughtered validly, but in practice it cannot be eaten.

and the same law applies to one who says to his slave etc.. But the solution in this case is more complicated, since a slave has no property of his own (see Hilchot Zechiyah 3:12), and therefore ordinarily he cannot take an additional kid or lamb for himself.

provided that his master's shepherd gives him etc.. A person from whom the master customarily buys animals gives him animals of both kinds, on condition that the extra animal be the slave's alone and not the master's (see there, halachot 13-14).
afterward it will be possible for the slave to stipulate as we explained. Only if he acts this way can the slave stipulate like a free agent, as above in the previous paragraph.

and he slaughtered and they slaughtered, they all eat from the one slaughtered first. In this case they appointed him as agent and he appointed them, and all fulfilled their obligation with the first one slaughtered in their name.
and the last one goes out to the place of burning. It is invalid, since it was slaughtered for people who were no longer obligated.
go and search and slaughter for us. Go and look for the lost Paschal offering, and they appointed him as agent to slaughter it for them.
and they took another Paschal offering and slaughtered it. And he did not appoint them as his agents.

if his was slaughtered first, he eats from his and they eat with him, and the second is burned. The searcher slaughtered the Paschal offering for them too, and they fulfilled their obligation with it, whereas the second Paschal offering was not slaughtered for those obligated in the Paschal offering.
and if theirs was slaughtered first, they eat from theirs and he eats from his. For each one slaughtered a Paschal offering for himself.
it is not known... he eats from his. For he slaughtered for himself, and they did not slaughter for him.

and they do not eat with him, and theirs goes out to the place of burning. Since there is doubt which is the offering slaughtered for them, they cannot eat from his and cannot eat their own. So their offering has no eaters, and therefore it is burned.
and they are exempt from observing the Second Pesach. For the Paschal offering was slaughtered validly, but it is not known which of them is the correct Paschal offering.

he said to them... if I am late, slaughter for me etc.. He appointed them as his agents, but they did not appoint him as their agent for slaughtering the Paschal offering. In this case the law is the reverse of the previous case.

a Paschal offering of theirs was lost and a Paschal offering of his was lost, and he said to them, "Go and search and slaughter for me" etc.. He appointed them as his agents and they appointed him, and therefore the one slaughtered first was slaughtered for all of them.
and they said nothing to one another. They did not appoint him, and he did not appoint them as agents.
for it was in their hearts etc.. They intended and hinted, but did not say explicitly.
they are not responsible for one another. There is no connection between them, and each eats for himself from the Paschal offering he slaughtered.
two groups whose Paschal offerings got mixed up. They do not know which lamb belongs to which group.
and one of the members of this group goes to those and one of the members of the second goes to the first. From each original group, one of those counted moves to the other group.

if this Paschal offering is ours, your hands are withdrawn from yours and you are counted for ours etc.. For so they stipulate, with the result that if the Paschal offerings were not switched, the new member is counted for this group's Paschal offering. And if the Paschal offerings were in fact switched, all the rest of the group were counted for the Paschal offering of the new member. The move of one person from each group to the other group is because a Paschal offering may not be left with no owners at all, and it is impossible to cancel the counting of all the members of the group, so one of them is left.
they withdraw one from each group to the other group. One from each group joins each of the Paschal offerings, so that in effect all the groups are split up.
and this one counts with him for his Paschal offering one from the marketplace. He adds another person and counts him for the lamb that is his Paschal offering, wherever he may be.
so that there be two groups. So that it will be possible to withdraw from the Paschal offering afterward and it will still have owners.
and afterward one of the two goes to those etc.. Afterward the people switch, and they follow the law of two groups whose Paschal offerings got mixed up, as mentioned above.
whose skins of their Paschal offerings got mixed up. After they were flayed from the sacrifices, and it is not known to which of them each skin belongs.
and a wart was found in the skin of one of them. A wart is a blemish (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:10), and it was discovered that one of the five offerings was invalid.
all of them go out to the place of burning. For it is forbidden to eat them, since this might be the invalid sacrifice.

and if they got mixed up before the sprinkling of their blood, they are obligated to observe the Second Pesach. For the offering was offered from the outset invalidly, since it is forbidden to eat because of the mixture (as above, halachah 2).

if they got mixed up after sprinkling, they are exempt from observing the Second Pesach. For if four of them were offered validly, it is not possible for all to bring a Second Pesach, as explained shortly.

this one who offered the first, a valid offering, brings unconsecrated animals into the Temple court. For he is not obligated in a Paschal offering, so the animal he brings as a Paschal offering is not consecrated but unconsecrated, and it is forbidden to slaughter unconsecrated animals in the Temple court (Hilchot Shechitah 2:1-3).

and if all were counted for one Paschal offering. In which case there would not be unconsecrated animals in the Temple court, since there is a group obligated in this offering, but there is another problem.

it turns out it was slaughtered for one who is not obligated etc.. The Paschal offering was slaughtered for those not obligated, that is, those groups that already fulfilled their obligation, and this is like a Paschal offering slaughtered for those counted and those not counted, which one does not do at the outset (see above 2:5).

and if each of them stipulated etc.. Even if they bring their offerings separately, and each group stipulates and says that if it is not obligated in a Second Pesach its offering shall be an ordinary peace offering, the stipulation does not help, for the manner of applying the blood of these offerings differs.
the blood of the Paschal offering by pouring. Onto the base of the altar (above 1:6).
and the blood of peace offerings by sprinkling. On two corners of the altar (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:6).

and those that are to be applied by sprinkling may not be applied by pouring at the outset. Only after the fact is it valid (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 2:1-2), and therefore they may not at the outset bring a Second Pesach.
it has already been explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 15:1-3, and see also there, halachah 11.
for the sake of the Paschal offering. And it is forbidden to slaughter it for the sake of another offering.
and for the sake of its owners. The members of the group counted for it.

and he told them after some time etc.. This speaks of a case where he could have told them earlier and did not, so his reliability is in doubt. But if he told them immediately upon seeing them, he is believed, since Israelites are not suspected of lying about this and forbidding what is permitted (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:15; and see also Hilchot Tefillin 1:18, Hilchot Ma'aser 12:18, Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 13:8).
the meat of the Paschal offering that became impure. And became forbidden to eat.

he does not sprinkle the blood, for the Paschal offering comes only for eating etc.. Although with other offerings it is permitted to sprinkle the blood if the meat became impure while the fats are pure (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:34), with the Paschal offering the law differs, for its purpose is the eating of its meat (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 7:5, and see below 7:8).
and if he did not know until the blood was sprinkled. If he sprinkled the blood unintentionally without knowing that the meat had become impure.

it was accepted. The tzitz atones after the fact for the sprinkling, and the offering is considered to have been offered validly. And although they are forbidden to eat the meat of the Paschal offering because it became impure, they are exempt from the Second Pesach, since it is as if the meat became impure after the blood was sprinkled (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
some of the limbs became impure. But pure limbs remain that can be eaten.

the fats became impure and the meat is intact, he sprinkles the blood etc.. If only the fats offered on the altar became impure and not the meat, the law is as with all offerings, and the offering is valid.
the owners became impure after it was slaughtered. And were thereby disqualified from eating the Paschal offering.
he does not sprinkle the blood etc.. For this offering has no owners fit to eat it (and this speaks of a case where all the owners became impure; see below, halachah 3).

for the tzitz does not atone for the impurity of the body unless he became impure with the impurity of the deep. The tzitz atones for a person's impurity only if he became impure with the impurity of the deep, a hidden corpse impurity that no one in the world knew about (Hilchot Nezirut 6:18-19, Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 7:7).
as we have explained in Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash. 4:6.
the Paschal offering that left Jerusalem. And became invalid and forbidden to eat, like the meat of any offering of lesser sanctity that left the wall of Jerusalem (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:6).
is burned immediately. Without needing to wait, for it is a positive commandment to burn consecrated items that became invalid (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:1).
until its form passes. One must wait until the meat spoils and is no longer fit for eating, and then burn it.

this is the rule: whatever is disqualified in its body is burned immediately. If the meat of the offering was disqualified because of mishaps that occurred to its body itself (such as having left or become impure), it is a severe disqualification, and therefore the meat can be burned immediately.

by the blood or by the owners, its form passes and afterward it is burned. When the offering was disqualified because of something external to it (the owners or impurity of the blood), the disqualification is lighter, and therefore one must wait for the meat to spoil and only then burn it (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).

if he slaughtered it after it was known that the owners had withdrawn their hands. The Paschal offering was slaughtered from the outset not for its eaters, and it is considered disqualified in its body.

when all the members of the group became impure. And there is no one besides them permitted to eat of the Paschal offering (for the Paschal offering is not eaten by those not counted for it, above 2:1).
the pure acquired the portion of the impure. In eating the meat that had been designated for them.
the pure who had not yet begun acquired. Since they had not yet received their portions, when they divide among themselves they also take the portion that was fit for the impure.
but if all began and some of them became impure etc.. In this case the portion of the impure is not distributed to the pure, since each had already acquired his portion (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
they burn it before the Birah. A place on the Temple Mount where they burn some consecrated items that became invalid (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:4).

in front of everyone, to shame them, so that they will be careful. Presumably they were negligent in guarding it from impurity, so the Sages enacted that it be burned in a place where the public sees, so they will learn to be careful in the future.

and they burn it with wood of the arrangement so that they will not be suspected etc.. They must burn the offering that became impure specifically with the wood of the altar arrangement, and not with unconsecrated wood they brought themselves, lest they take home the wood left over after the burning, and onlookers might think they are stealing from the wood of the arrangement.

if they burned it with reeds and straw etc.. Which are not used for the wood of the arrangement, only choice split wood (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 7:3), and therefore there is no problem of suspicion.
if a minority of it became impure, and likewise leftovers, they burn it in their courtyards with their own wood. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:7.

but not with the wood of the arrangement etc.. Although it was permitted to use the wood for burning invalid consecrated items, they did not permit taking some of it to their courtyards, lest they misuse what remains.
one who designates a female for his Paschal offering or a male two years old. Which are invalid for the Paschal offering, which must be male and within its first year (above 1:1).

it grazes until a blemish falls on it and it is sold. Although they are unfit for the Paschal offering, since they are unblemished they became consecrated with the sanctity of the body (Hilchot Temurah 1:21), so one waits until a blemish falls on them and then redeems them and they go out to unconsecrated status, and with their proceeds he brings an offering (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:10).

and if no blemish fell on it until he offered his Paschal offering, he brings peace offerings with the proceeds. For a Paschal offering that was deferred or left over is offered as a peace offering. The invalid animal itself is not offered as a peace offering (although in principle a female or a two-year-old is valid for that), because from the outset they were unfit for the offering for which they were designated, and therefore they may not be offered (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
one who designated his Paschal offering and died. And there were no other people counted for the Paschal offering.
his son may not bring it after him etc.. For no one counted for this Paschal offering remains, and it has the law of the remainder of a Paschal offering.
if his father died after midday on the fourteenth. The obligation of the Paschal offering fell on him from midday, before his father's death.
he is deferred to the Second Pesach because he is an onen. For at the time the obligation applied he was not fit to eat consecrated food, and therefore he is deferred to the Second Pesach.
as will be explained. Below 6:9.
and both of them are standing. And are fit to be offered.
and the second is offered as a peace offering. He offers the animal itself as a peace offering.

and likewise if he substituted for the one found after the slaughter. One who substitutes is one who consecrates an unconsecrated animal in exchange for a consecrated animal. The law is that the consecrated animal remains in its sanctity and the unconsecrated animal (the substitute) becomes consecrated and has the law of the original offering. If he substituted an unconsecrated animal for the lost Paschal offering and it was found after the other was slaughtered, the substitute is offered as a peace offering, just as this found Paschal offering is offered as a peace offering.
since this found animal is fit to be offered as a Paschal offering and fit to be offered as a peace offering, as we have explained. In the previous paragraph.

if he substituted for this found one, whether before the slaughter of the one designated in its place or after the slaughter, its substitute is not offered. Since the found animal for which he substituted was originally fit for the Paschal offering, its substitute is not offered and has the law of the substitute of a Paschal offering before midday, which grazes until a blemish falls on it, and he brings peace offerings with its proceeds (Hilchot Temurah 3:1; but if it had been completely deferred from the Paschal offering and its law were to be offered as a peace offering, its substitute too would itself be offered as a peace offering, as explained in the previous paragraph).
a Paschal offering whose year has passed. A lamb over a year old, which can no longer be brought as a Paschal offering but is offered as a peace offering.
and peace offerings that come on account of the Paschal offering. Under the laws mentioned in the previous halachot.

require laying on of hands, libations, and waving of the breast and thigh. The owners must lean their hands on the head of the offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:6), and bring libations of wine, oil, and flour with the offering (ibid. 2:2), and they set aside special portions from it for the priests and wave them (ibid. 9:6). All these laws apply to a peace offering and not to the Paschal offering.
a Paschal offering that got mixed with peace offerings. The animal was lost among other animals, and it is not possible to recognize which of them is the Paschal offering.
all of them are offered as peace offerings. For the Paschal offering too is offered as a peace offering after its time, so all have one law.
it got mixed with other sacrifices. Which differ in the way they are offered from peace offerings.

and he brings with the value of the best of them of this kind, and with the value of the best of them peace offerings etc.. He sells each one separately, and with the price of the most expensive of them brings the sacrifice he is obligated in, and likewise with that price a peace offering for the Paschal offering that got mixed with them.
and he loses the surplus. The difference between the sale price of the cheaper animal and the purchase of the expensive animal falls on the owners.
as we explained in Pesulei HaMukdashin. 6:6.

it got mixed with firstborns. A firstborn, when unblemished, is offered on the altar and eaten by the priests, and if blemished is eaten as unconsecrated meat without redemption and is the property of the priests (Hilchot Bechorot 1:2-3).

and they are eaten like a blemished firstborn. They are stringent with the meat of all the mixed animals according to the laws of a blemished firstborn, that it is forbidden to slaughter and sell it in the market and forbidden to weigh its meat on a scale as one weighs ordinary meat (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:12).

wherever it is the Paschal offering, its sanctity falls on this one. He desecrates the sanctity of the Paschal offering, but does not desecrate the sanctity of the firstborn, which is eaten without redemption and whose sanctity cannot be desecrated (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 6:12).
before he converted. While he was a gentile, and not obligated in the Paschal offering.
before he was freed and he was freed. He was a slave and was freed, and now is obligated as a free person.
before he grew two hairs and he grew. He was a minor and grew two hairs after age thirteen, which are signs of adulthood (Hilchot Ishut 2:10), and now is obligated as an adult.

for living animals are not deferred. Although there is a rule concerning consecrated things that something which was fit for offering and was deferred because of a particular disqualification is entirely disqualified even if the cause of the disqualification no longer exists ("seen and deferred, it is not seen again"), and by this rule the animal should have been deferred from being offered. However, this rule does not apply to animals while alive, and therefore they are not disqualified (and see further Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4 and the explanation there).
as we explained in Pesulei HaMukdashin. 3:23 and elsewhere.
one who sets aside money for his Paschal offering and had some left over. He consecrated a certain sum and ultimately bought the offering for less, and extra money remained in his hand.
one who counts others for his Paschal offering and his festival offering. He added them to be counted for an animal he consecrated.

even though this one set aside a lamb for his Paschal offering etc.. Although both the animal and the money are consecrated, and consecrated property is not redeemed with consecrated property but with unconsecrated, here the money goes out to unconsecrated status because it is clear that the money and the animal were consecrated from the outset so that the sanctity would ultimately rest only on the animal, and the money goes out to unconsecrated status.
wood for roasting the Paschal offering is like the Paschal offering. And it is permitted to buy it with the money he set aside for the Paschal offering, if some remained (Melekhet Mishneh).

and likewise matzah and bitter herbs, since they are accessories of the Paschal offering. For it is a commandment to eat the Paschal offering with matzot and bitter herbs (below 8:1-2), and therefore it is permitted to buy them with the money he set aside for the Paschal offering.

and if he took from the money of the Paschal offering from one whom he counted with him... the money is unconsecrated. If he received from those counted money from the money set aside for the Paschal offering, to include them in the matzah and bitter herbs or the wood for roasting the Paschal offering, the money goes out to unconsecrated status (like one who counts others for the Paschal offering itself, explained above, halachah 10).

one who was impure at the time of the slaughter of the Paschal offering, so that one does not slaughter for him. For example, one impure through contact with a corpse, or one who cannot become pure from his impurity by evening (to be explained below, chapter 6).
or on a distant journey. The distance will be explained below, halachah 9.
or was prevented by another circumstance. Another matter that entirely prevents him from the possibility of offering the Paschal offering.
on the fourteenth of the second month. That is the month of Iyar.

and the slaughter of this Paschal offering is a separate positive commandment. It is not part of the commandment of the first Pesach, but is considered a separate commandment (see Sefer HaMitzvot, positive commandment 57).

and it overrides Shabbat. Like the first Pesach (above 1:18), for of it too it says "in its appointed time" (Numbers 9:13; however in certain cases it does not override Shabbat; see below, halachah 8).
but a festival in itself, therefore they are liable to karet for it. As will be explained below.

one who erred or was prevented and did not offer on the first, if he deliberately did not offer on the second, is liable to karet. For although he is exempt for the first, for the second he is liable, since it is a festival in itself for one who did not fulfill his obligation with the first.
and if he erred or was prevented even on the second, he is exempt. For there is no punishment of karet for an unintentional or compelled violator.
if he deliberately did not offer on the first, he offers on the second. For he has a way to correct it at this time.
and if he did not offer on the second, even if he erred, he is liable to karet etc.. For the deliberate neglect of the first.

but one who was impure or on a distant journey... who was already exempted from the first Pesach from karet. For in this case he is exempt from the first Pesach and deferred to the Second Pesach. And of the second it says "but the man who is pure and not on a journey, and neglects to make the Pesach, that soul shall be cut off..." (Numbers 9:13), and one who was impure or on a distant journey is not included in this karet.
it was not accepted. Since the Torah entirely exempted him from the first Pesach.
an impure person who can become pure on the first Pesach. If he would immerse and become pure.
and likewise an uncircumcised person. Who is also forbidden to make the Paschal offering, and receives lashes for eating it (below 9:8).
he is deliberate with regard to the first. He is considered one who deliberately neglected, because he could have made himself permitted.
so too the circumcision of his minor sons. Who are under his authority, and it is his duty to circumcise them.
and the circumcision of all his slaves, whether adults or minors, prevents him. If he has slaves he must circumcise them (Hilchot Milah 1:1).

and likewise the immersion of his maidservants for the sake of servitude. When one buys a slave or maidservant from gentiles, he immerses them for the sake of servitude, as converts are immersed (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:11).
from tradition. A law transmitted by tradition.
for immersion for maidservants is like circumcision for slaves. They have one law, and it prevents the master from eating the Paschal offering.
a minor, the circumcision of his slaves does not etc.. A young child who has slaves and maidservants.
and any man's slave. A slave belonging to a man, that is, an adult.
are obligated to observe the Second Pesach. For the Second Pesach is a festival in itself, and obligates everyone who did not celebrate on the first (as above, halachah 1).
and if they slaughtered for him on the first, he is exempt. The minor, since it is permitted to count him for the Paschal offering even in his minority (as above 2:3-4).
the Second Pesach is optional for them. And not an obligation.
one does not slaughter for them by themselves on Shabbat for the Second Pesach. If there was a group entirely of women, since if the offering is not obligatory it does not override Shabbat.
fifteen mil. A mil is two thousand cubits, and in modern measures about a kilometer.
the day of the fourteenth with the rising of the sun. At sunrise of the fourteenth of Nisan.

since he can reach Jerusalem after midday if he walks at ease. A person can walk such a distance at a comfortable pace in about half a day (for the time to walk one mil is twenty-four minutes; Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 3:2).
because the animals delayed him with their crowding. For the roads were congested because of the pilgrims with their many animals.

he is prevented and is not on a distant journey. He is considered prevented and therefore deferred to the Second Pesach, but he is liable to karet if he deliberately neglects it (see above, halachah 2). And if they slaughtered for him and he arrived in the end, he has fulfilled his obligation (compare above, halachah 3).
imprisoned. Locked in prison.
they slaughter for him, and when he goes out in the evening he eats. For he is nearby.
when he was imprisoned by Israelites. For it can be assumed that they will keep their promise to release him.
if he was imprisoned by gentiles, they do not slaughter for him until he goes out. For one cannot know in advance whether he will truly be able to come.

who cannot eat etc.. Who eat little because of mourning or weakness, and one does not slaughter for them when they are in a group entirely of sick, elderly, or onanim. But it is permitted when they are counted in a group with others (above 2:4).
these are exempt from observing the Second Pesach. For they slaughtered for them at a time when they were fit to eat (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 8:6).

anyone who cannot eat the Paschal offering on the night of the fifteenth because of his impurity, such as zavim etc.. All of these must wait until the end of the days of their impurity, and only at the end become pure to eat consecrated food.
but one who touched a carcass or a creeping creature and the like etc.. For if they immerse they become pure that same evening.
and they slaughter for him after he immerses. He must perform the necessary action on his part, the immersion in a mikveh, so that he will certainly be pure on the night the offering is eaten.

and at night when his sun sets. After the sun sets and three stars emerge (see Hilchot Terumot 7:2), when the purification of the impure is completed. And until then, even though he has already immersed to become pure from the impurity, he is called a tevul yom and is still considered impure for several matters in halachah (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 10:1).

one impure from a corpse whose seventh day falls on the fourteenth. The seventh day is the last day of his impurity, on which the water of the red heifer's ashes is sprinkled on him, he immerses, and becomes pure in the evening (Hilchot Parah 11:1).

they learned from tradition that it was their seventh. It is the Sages' tradition to be precise that only on that day, at the time of offering the Paschal offering ("on that day"), they were not pure, but in the evening they could be pure.

and about this they asked whether one slaughters for them etc.. Their dilemma was whether the law of one impure from a corpse on the seventh day is like that of one impure from a creeping creature, so that if he did all the acts of purification one may slaughter for him and he eats in the evening, or not.

and it was explained to them that one does not slaughter for them. For the impurity of a corpse is more severe than other impurities, in that even after he is sprinkled and immerses he is still called impure from a corpse, and one does not slaughter for him (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
when he became impure with impurities of a corpse for which a nazirite shaves. As detailed in Hilchot Nezirut 7:2.

but if he was impure with other impurities of a corpse for which a nazirite does not shave etc.. These impurities were detailed there, halachah 6, and although in them too a person becomes impure for seven days and requires sprinkling of the ashes of the red heifer (ibid., halachah 7), their law is not as severe as other corpse impurities, and therefore here their law is like the other impure persons for whom one slaughters on the basis that they will be pure in the evening (for another law in which these impurities are lighter than other corpse impurities see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:13-14).

a zav who had two sightings. Two sightings of a discharge, and in this state he must count seven clean days, immerse on the seventh day, and become pure in the evening (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 3:1).

and counted seven days and immersed on the seventh, one slaughters for him and he eats in the evening. Like other impure persons who immersed on the last day of their impurity, for whom one slaughters since they are fit to eat the Paschal offering in the evening.

and if he saw a discharge after the blood was sprinkled, he is exempt from observing the Second Pesach. When a zav sees a discharge on the seventh day, even if he saw it after he immersed, the law is that it cancels all seven days, and he must count them anew (ibid.), and therefore he cannot eat the Paschal offering in the evening. But since he saw the discharge after the blood was sprinkled, he is exempt from the Second Pesach. The commentators found this law difficult, since this zav is considered impure retroactively and it turns out he was not fit to eat at the time the blood was sprinkled. Some explained that this situation is treated as the impurity of the deep, unknown to a person (see below, halachot 11-12), for here too no one in the world knew of it at the time of offering, and the impurity of the deep was permitted regarding the Paschal offering (see Tzlach, Pesachim 81a, and others who followed him). Others suggested that he is judged as if he were fit to eat of the Paschal offering in the evening (as above, halachah 1), for had he not seen the discharge he would indeed have been permitted to eat in the evening, and the sighting is by chance and not necessary (Or Sameach there and in his novellae on Nazir 63a).

and likewise a woman who keeps a day for a day etc.. A woman who saw blood during her days of zivah for a day or two, and must keep the next day in purity, and immerses that day and is pure in the evening.
as we explained in Issurei Bi'ah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:7-10.

and if she saw blood after the blood of the Paschal offering was sprinkled, she is exempt from observing the Second Pesach. If she saw during the day of keeping, even after she immersed, she is retroactively impure (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav U'Moshav 5:6). Therefore she is forbidden to eat the Paschal offering, but exempt from the Second Pesach, like the zav who saw after immersing.
and one does not slaughter for a niddah on her seventh. On the seventh day of her impurity.

for she does not immerse until the night of the eighth etc.. Unlike a zav and a zavah, who immerse on the seventh day of their purification, a niddah immerses only in the evening after completing seven days of her niddah (ibid. 4:6), and then she is a tevulat yom and must wait until the next evening (the night of the ninth) for it to be permitted for her to eat consecrated food.

those lacking atonement. A zav, a zavah, a woman after childbirth, and a metzora, who after they immersed and the sun set must bring an offering to permit them to eat consecrated food (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
one slaughters for them. The Paschal offering, for after bringing the offering that permits them they will be permitted to eat consecrated food.

and they offer their sacrifices on the fourteenth, whether before the slaughter of the Paschal offering or after its slaughter. Although ordinarily offerings are not slaughtered after the afternoon daily offering, in this case it was permitted so that they would be permitted to eat the Paschal offering in the evening (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 1:3-4).

and one does not slaughter for them until they hand over their sacrifices to the court. Only if they deposit the sacrifices with the court of priests is there no doubt that the priests will offer them; but if they did not hand them over, there is concern that the priests will be negligent and not offer them, and the Paschal offering would turn out to have been slaughtered for one not fit to eat it.
as we explained in Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash. 3:6.

a positive commandment that carries karet comes and overrides a prohibition of their own enactment. The commandment of the Paschal offering, whose neglect carries the penalty of karet (above 1:2), overrides the prohibition the Sages decreed against a tevul yom entering the Women's Court.
a metzora whose eighth day falls. Which is the day of bringing his offerings.
he immerses. To become pure from the impurity of a seminal emission; he is still a tevul yom until the sun sets.

and enters the Women's Court and brings his offerings. For a metzora must stand, while his offerings are brought, in the Women's Court at the entrance of the Israelites' Court, to lean on his offerings and so that the priest can perform on him the ceremony of his purification, which includes applying the offering's blood and oil to his ear and the thumb of his right hand and foot (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).
they sprinkle on him only on the next day. For sprinkling the purification waters on Shabbat is forbidden as a shevut (Hilchot Shabbat 23:8); rather, they sprinkle on Sunday.
and they sprinkle on him and do not slaughter for him. Like a tevul yom of corpse impurity.
as we explained. Above, halachah 2.

but is not the prohibition of sprinkling on Shabbat a shevut etc.. It is puzzling: why do they refrain from sprinkling on the seventh day when it falls on Shabbat, when this is only a shevut prohibition, and thereby cause the neglect of the commandment of the Paschal offering, whose neglect carries karet?
it is not the time of the offering for which they are liable to karet. For the day of sprinkling is the thirteenth of Nisan, which is not the time of the Paschal offering.

even though this causes in the future to stand in place of karet. The Sages did not set aside their own enactments on account of Torah commandments that will be done in the future, but only when one is liable for them now.
an uncircumcised Israelite who circumcised on the eve of Pesach. And thereby was made fit to eat the Paschal offering.
but a convert who converted... one does not slaughter for him, for he does not eat in the evening. For in this case he is forbidden to eat of the Paschal offering by rabbinic decree, as below.
like one who separates from a grave. As if he became impure through a corpse.

a decree lest this convert become impure through a corpse the following year on the fourteenth etc.. At the time of conversion he performed no act of purification other than the immersion of conversion (for by Torah law gentiles are not impure with any impurity; see Hilchot Tumat Met 1:13), and he might conclude from this that in the following year too immersion alone suffices, even if he became impure through a corpse.

and how did they uphold their words in place of karet on the day of the offering, which is the fourteenth. Here too it is puzzling why a rabbinic decree should set aside an important positive commandment of the Torah on the day of the offering itself (compare above, halachah 6).

because a convert is not obligated in commandments until he circumcises and immerses. Only after these two acts does he become obligated in the commandments like an Israelite (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:1-6).
until he heals from the circumcision. Until the wound heals completely.
as we explained regarding conversion. There, 14:5.

therefore they upheld their words in this case etc.. The Sages decreed to defer this convert from the Paschal offering because a convert's obligation in the Paschal offering is not absolute, for in principle the time of immersion can be postponed for other reasons such as medical ones, and as long as he has not immersed his conversion is not complete and he is not obligated in any commandment. Therefore even where he moved up the immersion, the Sages deferred him, as a decree because of the following year.

one who entered a beit haperas. He needed to walk in a field in which a grave was plowed and the bones of the dead were scattered in its soil, and the Sages decreed that its soil conveys impurity by contact and carrying, lest it contain a bone the size of a barley grain (which is the measure of a bone that conveys impurity as a corpse).
blowing and walking, blowing and walking. He blows with his mouth on the dust of the road to see whether any bone is buried in it.
as will be explained in Hilchot Tumat Met. 2:16 (and further on the laws of beit haperas there, chapter 10).
as we explained. Above, halachah 5.

a beit haperas that was threshed is pure for one who makes the Paschal offering. For many people walked there, and we assume that by the trampling of feet the bones in it were removed and broken. With regard to the Paschal offering the Sages did not decree to be concerned that impurity-conveying bones might still remain.

an onen is fit to eat the Paschal offering in the evening because nighttime aninut is rabbinic. An onen is one whose close relative, for whom he is obligated to mourn, has died, and he is forbidden to eat consecrated food and to perform the Temple service. On the day of death he is an onen by Torah law, and on the following night and on the days after until the deceased is buried he is an onen by rabbinic law (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:6, Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 2:9-10).

they did not uphold their words in this matter in place of karet. Since by Torah law he became obligated to bring the Paschal offering even before the relative died, they did not enact a prohibition on eating consecrated food at night.

and immerses and afterward eats, so that he separates from his aninut and does not forget. The Sages enacted immersion for consecrated food for an onen who finished his aninut, out of concern that he forgot about impurity during the time he was forbidden consecrated food (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 12:15). Therefore he immerses to separate from his aninut and be mindful from now on not to become impure.

but if the deceased died before midday, one does not slaughter for him. For when the time of obligation arrived he was already an onen, and in such a case the Sages upheld their words not to cancel nighttime aninut, and they deferred him to the Second Pesach.

and if they slaughtered for him and sprinkled the blood, he immerses and eats in the evening. For by Torah law he is fit to eat at night, and they permitted him to eat it so that the Paschal offering not be disqualified (Or Sameach).
on the day of burial he is an onen by rabbinic law. All that day, even after the burial.

and his night does not take hold, not even by rabbinic law. He is not considered an onen even by rabbinic law, since the Sages did not enact nighttime aninut for the day of burial, only for the day of death.
even with other consecrated offerings. Although there is no karet penalty for neglecting them.
and the day of the report. When he heard that his relative died elsewhere, and he observes mourning from that day (see Hilchot Avel 7:1-3).
and the day of gathering the bones. On which they gather the bones to bring them to permanent burial, and mourning customs are observed (see ibid. 12:8).
it is like the day of burial. For he is an onen on them by rabbinic law, during the day and not at night.
one who digs in the heap to search for the dead. Clears a pile of fallen stones to look for a person who died beneath it so as to bring him to burial.
they slaughtered for him and no corpse was found there. It turned out that there was no person there.
for example, if the heap was round. That all the stones were gathered together over the corpse, so that he certainly overshadowed the corpse.

and if it is doubtful, and perhaps he was not standing over the impurity at the time of sprinkling. For example, with an elongated heap, where the corpse may have been at another side of the heap and he did not overshadow it until after the time of sprinkling.
and a corpse was found lying across the width of a road. Buried beneath the road, so that everyone passing on the road overshadows the corpse.
if the corpse was an impurity of the deep. An impurity unknown to anyone in the world (see above 4:2).

even though he is impure with regard to terumah. For he is presumed impure with regard to terumah. This is not considered a doubtful impurity, which is pure in a public domain (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 18:3).
for it is possible that he did not touch. And in such a case they declared the impurity of the deep pure for one who makes the Paschal offering.
because it is impossible that he did not touch, carry, or overshadow. And he certainly became impure.
in Hilchot Nezirut. 6:18-19.
and afterward he learned that he had been impure with the impurity of the deep etc.. In this case, even if he was certainly impure with the impurity of the deep, he is exempt from the Second Pesach.
a law from tradition. Known in the Sages' tradition.
and was sprinkled on the third and the seventh. And afterward immersed.

he is not obligated in the Second Pesach, for once he immersed on the seventh day, the first impurity ceased. For he is no longer impure from a corpse (but a tevul yom until the sun sets), and at the time he made the Paschal offering he was presumed pure.

for the presumption of one who is impure is that he is impure until he is certainly pure. One who was presumed impure is not considered pure until it is clarified with certainty that he was in fact purified.
for there is a basis for the matter. We assume the situation as it was known (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 9:2).
a minority of the congregation. The minority of those making the Paschal offering (for how to check whether it is a majority or a minority see below, halachah 6).
these are deferred to the Second Pesach like the other impure persons. Although they are many people, their law is that of an individual deferred to the Second Pesach (above 5:1).
service vessels. The vessels used for offering.

"And there were men etc.". The continuation of the verse: "who were impure through the soul of a man and could not make the Pesach on that day..." For this case the law of the Second Pesach was innovated, and from the word "men" it is inferred that only individuals are deferred, not the community.
with the impurity of a corpse only. Which alone is set aside in the Temple, in offerings with a fixed time.
as we explained in Bi'at HaMikdash. 4:9, 4:12.
the congregation was half pure and half impure from a corpse. That they were divided exactly in half.
all make it on the first etc.. For each half is considered the majority of the congregation and makes it for itself (Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 79a).
and they eat it in impurity. They are permitted to eat the Paschal offering in their impurity, since it comes originally for eating (below, halachah 8).
even one. The impure outnumber the pure even by a single person.
all of them make it in impurity. Even the pure, who need not be careful about the purity of the meat and the priests.
and when you count the women among the men, the majority are pure. For the pure women outnumbered the impure.
the pure make the first. For they are the majority of the community.
for women are optional regarding the Second. As above 5:8, and therefore they are not counted in the count for the Second Pesach, with the result that there is half the congregation there.
and half do not make the Second. For half is treated as a majority (above, halachah 2).
zavim, metzoraim, and those who had relations with niddot. Impure with impurities other than corpse impurity, who cannot become pure that same evening.
those impure from a corpse do not make the first because they are a minority. For those impure with other impurities are not combined with those impure from a corpse to form a majority of the impure.
and here, since they did not make it. For the majority were impure with various impurities.
those impure from a corpse make the first. As the law of the majority of the congregation, which overrides impurity.
for only the impurity of a corpse is set aside for the community. As above, halachah 1.
but if the first was made in impurity, there is no Second Pesach. For only a first Pesach made in purity defers to the Second Pesach those who could not make it.
and they do not make the Second, for a minority made the first. For only if the majority made the first are the rest deferred to the Second Pesach.
as we explained. Above, halachah 4.
how do they assess the Paschal offering. To count the number of the pure and the impure.

they do not assess among all the eaters etc.. They do not check how many of the congregation who are to eat the Paschal offering are impure or pure, but follow those who offer the sacrifice (compare Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:12).
and while they are outside, before the first group enters, they assess them. They check all those about to offer, even before they divide into three groups (as above 1:9).

an individual who became impure with a doubt in a private domain. That there is doubt whether he touched corpse impurity. The rule is that when the doubt arose in a private domain the person is considered impure.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 15:8.

and a community that became impure with a doubt in a private domain, all make it in impurity. There is no difference in this matter between an individual and the community, and the community too is considered impure in a case of doubtful impurity in a private domain.

a Paschal offering that they offered in impurity is eaten as if pure. They eat its meat just as they eat a pure Paschal offering. This is unlike other offerings that come in impurity, where only the offering overrides the impurity but not the eating, and their meat is burned (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 4:11).
for from the outset it comes only for eating. For the essence of the Paschal offering is its eating, and therefore eating it in impurity was permitted when it was offered in impurity.

and similar to them, those impure by contact impurities. Those similar in their impurity to those impure from a corpse in that they became impure through something external to their body (such as one impure from a creeping creature or from touching a zav).
they learned from tradition. The Sages' tradition of interpreting the verses (see Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 95b).

even if those impure from a corpse ate of their fats they are exempt. Although the fats (the parts of the offering that go up on the altar) are forbidden to eat for everyone (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:3), and an impure person who eats them is liable to karet (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:18), here he is exempt from karet for the impurity because it was permitted to make it in impurity.

but if they became impure after the blood was sprinkled, it is not eaten. It is forbidden to eat it in impurity, for this Paschal offering was made in purity and its law is to be eaten in purity, since eating the Paschal offering in impurity was not permitted in itself, but only for a Paschal offering whose essential making was in impurity.

and the Paschal offering is not eaten, a decree lest they become impure after sprinkling in another year and eat it in impurity. Although by law it would be permitted to eat it in impurity, since the blood was sprinkled when the majority were impure, they nonetheless forbade it out of concern for confusion in later years.

those impure from a creeping creature and the like, since they do not make a person impure. For a vessel that became impure with a primary source of impurity (such as a creeping creature) makes impure only food and drink.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7.
only the pure make it etc.. They do not permit the impure to offer the Paschal offering, even though the pure who offer will ultimately have to eat impure meat.

better that it be eaten with the impurity of meat, which is a prohibition, than that those impure in their body, who are subject to karet, eat it. For the prohibition of eating impure meat is lighter than eating meat while impure in one's body.
as we explained in Pesulei HaMukdashin. 18:12-13.
and matzah and bitter herbs do not prevent. Rather, eating the Paschal offering is a commandment in itself.

but bitter herbs without a Paschal offering are not a commandment. By rabbinic law it is a commandment to eat them even when there is no Paschal offering (Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 7:12). Eating matzah, however, is a commandment in itself, and one is obligated in it by Torah law even without the Paschal offering (ibid. 6:1).
eating to satiety. That he eat of it until he is full and does not want to eat afterward. For this is the way with important foods (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
if he offered the festival peace offerings on the fourteenth. Which is an optional offering (see below 10:12-13).
and if he ate only an olive-bulk he fulfills his obligation. Even if he ate a small amount of the Paschal offering he fulfills his obligation, since that is the measure of eating everywhere.
both. The first Paschal offering and the second.
are eaten only roasted over fire. It is permitted to eat the meat only if it was roasted over fire, as will be explained in the following halachot.
raw. Meat that was roasted slightly and is still not fit for human consumption (below, halachah 6).
boiled. In liquids (below, halachah 7).

since both are included in one prohibition. For no separate prohibitory language was designated for each of them (it was not said "do not eat it raw and do not eat it cooked") but for both together (and see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:3).
while it is still day. Before the time of its eating, which is at night.
at night and not by day. From the fact that it says the meat must be eaten specifically at night, it can be inferred that it is forbidden to eat it by day.

and a prohibition derived from a positive commandment is a positive commandment. A prohibition not stated in the Torah in negative language but learned as the converse of a positive commandment is like a positive commandment, for which one does not receive lashes.
raw meat. Not cooked at all in any manner.
he roasted it as much as he needed until it was charred. He roasted it entirely until burned.
and he ate it, he is exempt. For it is still within "roasted over fire."
and "cooked, cooked" includes everything. From the repetition we learn to forbid cooking in all kinds of liquids.
roasted in a pot. He cooked it in a pot without adding liquids.
and ate it, he is liable. For all of these were also included in cooking.
but it is permitted to smear it with wine, oil, and other liquids and fruit juices. To smear them on it before roasting, since they are not meant to cook it but to give the meat flavor.
except for water. Which gives no flavor and resembles cooking (Malkhei BaKodesh).
on stone vessels or metal vessels. For the vessel separates the meat from the fire.
not roasted by something else. And here the Paschal offering is roasted by the heat of the vessel and not by the heat of the fire.
so that the fire has power over it. So that the heat of the fire itself reaches the meat through the holes of the vessel.
for the spit is hot all over and roasts its place. If the spit heats up at one end, all of it becomes hot, and meat not reached by the heat of the fire is cooked by the spit and not by the fire.
and swept out all the fire. He removed the coals from the oven, and the oven is still hot from that heating.
he cut it up and roasted it on coals. And not when whole and inside an oven.
lime or clay. Building materials whose mixture with water produces a great deal of heat.
the hot springs of Tiberias. Water that gushes from the ground hot, and he cooked with the heat that rises from them.
for this is not roasting over fire. But another source of heat.
he pierces it from its mouth to its rear opening. He thrusts a long spit through the whole lamb, from its head to its rear.
of wood. And not of metal, as above, halachah 9.

and hangs its legs and innards in the oven outside it, and does not put them inside it etc.. He hangs the inner organs on the spit outside the lamb and does not leave them inside it, since then they would not roast directly from the fire.
and a pomegranate spit. A long branch of the pomegranate tree.
so that it not discharge its moisture and cook it. For in other woods there is moisture in the joints of the branch, which may be released during roasting and cause cooking.
the meat touched the clay of the oven. The body of the oven, made of clay, which is very hot from the fire and roasts the meat that touches it.
he must peel off its place. He must remove the outer part of the meat that touched the body of the oven.
its juices dripped onto the clay. Liquids came out of the meat because of the roasting, reached the clay of the oven, and splashed back onto the meat.
he must peel off its place. He must remove the outer part onto which the juices splashed.

for all the gravy and liquid that separates from it when it is roasted is forbidden, since it is not roasted meat. For it is forbidden to eat from the Paschal offering the liquids that come out of it during roasting, only its meat.
he must scoop out its place and throw it away. He removes the flour in which the gravy was absorbed, for it is forbidden to eat this gravy.
he smeared it with oil of terumah. He spread on it terumah oil, which is forbidden to eat for one who is not a priest.

if it is raw, he rinses it and dries it. If the Paschal offering has not yet been roasted, the meat can be washed in water. Afterward he must dry it of the water, for it is forbidden to smear it with water before roasting, as above, halachah 8 (Malkhei BaKodesh, Har HaMoriah).
and if it is roasted, he peels off the outer part. For what was smeared on the roasted meat was absorbed slightly into it, and became forbidden to eat for one who is not a priest.
he may not turn it into money from the members of the group. The owner may not request the price of the oil from the other members of the group.

for second tithe is not redeemed in Jerusalem. When money is taken for the oil, it is considered a redemption of the oil with the money (transferring the sanctity of the tithe to the money), and this is forbidden because produce of the tithe is not redeemed after it enters Jerusalem.
as we explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:8.
and two Paschal offerings are not roasted as one. In an oven together.
because of mixing. Lest the offerings get switched with one another, and the Paschal offering end up eaten by people not counted for it.
even a kid and a lamb. Although there is no practical concern that they will be switched, since they differ from one another.
we have already explained in several places that the Paschal offering is eaten only until midnight. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:8, Pesulei HaMukdashin 6:12.

to keep far from transgression etc.. Although anything whose commandment is at night is valid by Torah law all night (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:6), the Sages made a safeguard and set that it be eaten only until midnight, so that he not be drawn on until the end of the time (for similar safeguards see Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:9, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:2).
and we have already explained in Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah that it requires Hallel at the time of eating. 8:5, 8:10; and see below 10:15.
and that the members of the group do not return and eat after they fell asleep. Hilchot Chametz U'Matzah 8:14.
he eats only in one group. The eater may be in only one place in one group, as will be explained below.
and one does not take out any of it etc.. It is forbidden to move the meat outside the group.
and this is only if he leaves it outside. He is liable to lashes only if he took it out and ultimately left it there, and not if he moved it without leaving it.

for taking out is written regarding it as with Shabbat.
