On Shabbat carrying from domain to domain was forbidden, based on the verse "let no man leave his place on the seventh day" (Exodus 16:29), and the prohibition of moving the meat of the Paschal offering from place to place is likewise called "taking out" in the Torah.
requires lifting and placing, like taking out on Shabbat. For one is liable for carrying from domain to domain only for lifting from one domain and placing in the other (Hilchot Shabbat 13:1).

and there is no one who takes out after one who takes out with the Paschal offering. If after the meat was taken out, the meat returned to its place and was taken out again, the second is not liable, since the meat was disqualified by the first removal.
from the door-hinge inward is like inside. The area from the end of the thickness of the inner doorway toward the inside of the house is considered inside.
and the door-hinge area itself, the thickness of the doorway. The space of the doorway.
the windows and the thickness of the walls are like inside. These spaces are considered the interior of the house.
the roofs and upper rooms are not included in the house. And if he took some of the meat out there, he receives lashes.

and it is like the meat of the most holy offerings that left the Temple court etc.. For any meat that left the partition appropriate to it is disqualified and forbidden forever like a treifah (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 5:9), as it says "you shall not eat flesh torn in the field" (Exodus 22:30), and the Sages expounded: "once meat has left its partition, it becomes like a treifah."
as we explained in Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. 11:6.
a limb partly taken out. That was placed partly outside its partition, with part still inside.
he cuts the meat and removes it etc.. Only the meat that left is forbidden, and therefore it must be separated from the permitted meat.
he cuts with a cleaver if it was other consecrated offerings. He chops the bone with a butcher's knife to remove the entire part that left and became forbidden.
if it was other consecrated offerings. Offerings other than the Paschal offering, for which breaking bones was not forbidden.
a Paschal offering in which it is forbidden to break a bone. As below 10:1.
he peels up to the joint and disjoints the limb etc.. He separates the permitted meat from the bone up to the nearby joint, cuts the bones apart at the joint, and throws away the whole bone.
each group among them must make itself a partition. A partition delimiting their place of eating (see below, halachah 5).
and these turn their faces this way and eat etc.. Each group must eat with its members' faces turned away from the other group.
the water in which they mix their wine was in the middle of the house. During the meal it is necessary to bring some of this water to dilute the wine.
when the attendant stands to mix. And to bring water to the members of his group from the place between the groups.
closes his mouth and turns his face. He closes his mouth and stops eating, and keeps his face turned toward his own group, so that he will not appear to be eating in the other group.
and the bride is permitted to turn her face etc.. To turn her face in another direction.

whose partition between them broke. There had been a partition surrounding them, and it broke after they began eating the offering; they are forbidden to continue eating because they are not separated from the other group (as above, halachah 3).
and a partition was made between them. A partition was set up between the members of the group.

for the Paschal offering is not eaten in two groups, and one does not move from group to group. Because of the making of the partition they are considered another group, and it is forbidden to move from one group to another (the words "the Paschal offering is not eaten in two groups" are a remnant of the first edition of the Rambam, who originally held that the Paschal offering may not be eaten in two groups; see Birkat Avraham and the notes of Rabbi Yitzchak Shilat in Rambam Meduyak, and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained the reading before us).
and the one who calls returned to all of them for the rest. The appointed person went around and called the rest of the group members to gather.
they eat until they are satisfied and do not wait for the rest. And they are permitted to eat as much as they want, even more than their proportional share of the offering.
and these three who ate everything found... they do not pay them the value of their share. Because they had permission to eat as much as they wanted, since the others did not arrive.
but if only two entered, they wait. They must wait.
but at the time they depart. When they leave the meal.
a person need not wait for his fellow etc.. They may leave the group at any time they wish, and need not wait for everyone to finish eating (see Kesef Mishneh).
to an apostate to idolatry. An Israelite who worships idols.

or to a resident alien or a hired worker. A gentile who accepted upon himself not to worship idols and to keep the seven Noahide commandments, and has permission to reside in the Land of Israel (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7), or who is an Israelite's hired worker.
he transgresses a negative commandment and does not receive lashes. Because it is a prohibition with no act, as the one who feeds did no act himself but caused others to eat (Meiri, Yevamot 71a).
but they give him lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by rabbinic law for violating a prohibition.

and the "foreigner" mentioned in the Torah is one who worships a foreign god etc.. The expression "ben nekhar" refers to an Israelite who is an apostate to idolatry, and not to a gentile, whose prohibition is learned from the phrase "resident and hired worker."
uncircumcised. An Israelite who was not circumcised.
but he eats matzah and bitter herbs. For he is obligated in them, even though they come with the Paschal offering, as they are separate commandments (above 8:2).
and likewise it is permitted to feed matzah and bitter herbs to a resident alien and a hired worker. For in this they do not have the law of the Paschal offering.

just as the circumcision of his sons and slaves prevents him from slaughtering the Paschal offering. If one of them is uncircumcised, the son's father or the slave's owner may not slaughter (above 5:5).

how: he bought a slave etc.. In this way it is possible that he slaughtered the Paschal offering permissibly, without having had uncircumcised sons and slaves, and only at the time of eating he had them and was forbidden to eat because of them.

for example, if the heat took hold of him, so that he needs seven days of twenty-four hours from the day of his recovery. That his body heat rose, and one waits seven full days from the time he recovered, and afterward circumcises him (Hilchot Milah 1:16). If the time is completed between the slaughter of the Paschal offering and its eating, it turns out that the father became obligated in circumcision at that time, and it forbids him to eat the Paschal offering if he did not circumcise his son.

or he was a tumtum and was torn open after the slaughter of the Paschal offering and found to be male. A tumtum is one whose sex is unclear, male or female. But if his body was opened and it was discovered he is male, he is uncircumcised and forbids his father to eat the Paschal offering until he circumcises him. [Note: in the Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes this word as tumtum.]
but a Paschal offering that came in impurity. When most of the community is impure and they offer and eat the Paschal offering in impurity (above 7:1).
in which he broke a bone while it was still day. Although the time of eating had not yet arrived.
or broke after several days. Although it was already disqualified and became leftover.

therefore they burn the bones of the Paschal offering together with the leftover of its meat, so that they not come to a mishap with them. Although with other offerings only the meat and bones with marrow are burned from the leftover (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:9), with the Paschal offering they burn all the bones so that they not come to the prohibition of breaking a bone (and although the next halachah explains that for bones without marrow one is not liable for breaking a bone, because of the concern for mishap they did not distinguish among the bones and all must be burned; see Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon, who discusses this and explains in various ways).
and one who breaks after one who breaks a bone. One who breaks a bone that was already broken.
and one who cuts sinews is not liable for breaking a bone. Although they are hard and not fit for eating like bones, they are not included in the prohibition.
raw. That was not roasted as much as needed and is not fit for eating.
or cooked. And it is forbidden to eat it since it is not roasted (above 8:4).
and taking out. Outside its group (above 9:2).
when it had a time of validity and was disqualified. That the offering was made validly and afterward disqualified.

that became piggul or was made with the intention of time. A piggul intention is an intention to eat or offer the offering after its time, which disqualifies the offering (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1). Therefore the expression "or was made with the intention of time" is difficult. Some emend to "or was made with the intention of place" (Ben Aryeh, Aruch HaShulchan 194:11), for an intention to offer or eat the offering outside its place also disqualifies the offering (ibid.).
an intention of changing the name. That it was slaughtered not for the sake of the Paschal offering or not for its owners, and it is invalid (ibid. 15:1).
the bone of the fat tail. The bone in the lamb's tail, which is burned on the altar and not eaten.
the cartilages... these are permitted to eat. They are not considered bones, and therefore eating them does not involve the prohibition of breaking a bone.
a small, tender kid whose bones are soft. And fit for eating.
in a large ox. Whose bones are hard.
the tips of the wings. The sinews around the joints between the bones (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 7:11).
fit for eating now. While they are soft.
and are eaten with the Paschal offering. For they have no prohibition of breaking a bone (above, halachah 5).

one is not counted for them. There must be an olive-bulk of meat in the Paschal offering for each of those counted (above 2:14), and although it is possible to eat the sinews, they are not considered meat, and one cannot rely on them to add more people to the Paschal offering.
and one is counted for the brain in the head, since he can take it out without breaking a bone. He can take it out through the nostrils without breaking the skull bone.
and he cuts the bones at the joint and disjoints them. It is permitted to separate the bones from one another at their joint.
the sciatic nerve. Which is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 8:1).
the other sinews, bones, and membranes that come out at the time of eating. Which are not fit for eating.

for it is not cleaned like other meat. Unlike meat from which the sciatic nerve and the other forbidden sinews and fats must be removed before cooking or roasting, the Paschal offering is not cleaned this way before roasting because it is roasted whole (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).

and if he cut it into pieces it is valid, provided that he did not lack a limb. Although there is a commandment to roast it whole, if he cut it into several pieces it is valid, on condition that he leaves the limbs whole (Chazon Ish, Pesachim 5:10, who wrote that this is out of concern for breaking a bone).
and likewise the Second. The Second Pesach, and the same applies to the meat of all offerings (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:9).

for it was converted into a positive commandment. The negative prohibition ("you shall not leave over") was shifted to become a positive commandment ("you shall burn with fire"), and one does not receive lashes for it.
like all peace offerings. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:11.
and this is called the fourteenth festival offering. It is eaten before the Paschal offering in order to eat the Paschal offering when satiated (above 8:3).
and when few. That there were few Paschal offerings and consequently many had to be counted for one Paschal offering, which is not enough for satiety (Meiri, Pesachim 69b).
is eaten for two days and one night. Until sunset on the fifteenth.
like all peace offerings. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:6.
and one who leaves over does not receive lashes. Since it is a prohibition converted to a positive commandment (see above, halachah 11).
rather, the leftover of it is burned like other leftovers. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:1.
are burned with it. If they remained after midnight.

and they are eaten only until midnight etc.. Since he brings them up with the Paschal offering on one table, there is concern that some of the Paschal offering's meat will be mixed in them, and therefore their eating is treated as with the Paschal offering.
the first is forbidden with chametz, under "it shall not be seen" and "it shall not be found," and is not slaughtered while chametz is present. Above 1:5.
and one does not take any of it outside the group. Above 9:1.
and it requires Hallel at its eating. Above 8:15.
and they bring a festival offering with it. Above, halachah 12.
and it can come in impurity if most of the congregation became impure from a corpse. Above 7:1.
chametz and matzah with it in the house. Although it must be eaten with matzah (above 8:3), it is not forbidden with chametz.
and one takes it out of the place of its eating. It is not disqualified when taken out of its group and the house in which it is eaten.
and both override Shabbat. Above 1:16; 5:1.
and require Hallel in their making. Above 1:11.
and are eaten roasted. Above 8:4.
in one house. Although the meat of the Second Pesach is not disqualified when it leaves the house and its group, it must be returned and its eating finished in the same house (Rabbi Yitzchak Kolon).
and one does not leave any of it over. Above, halachah 11.
and one does not break a bone in them. Above, halachah 1.

for it specified some of the statutes of the Paschal offering. As detailed before this: "they shall eat it with matzot and bitter herbs; they shall not leave any of it until morning, and they shall not break a bone of it" (Numbers 9:11-12).
the commandments in its body. Commandments that apply to the body of the offering itself, and not matters that accompany it.
in Egypt. In the Paschal offering made at the Exodus from Egypt.
from the tenth. They took the Paschal offering on the tenth of Nisan (Exodus 12:3).
applying blood with a bunch of hyssop to the lintel and the two doorposts. They dipped a bunch of hyssop stalks in the offering's blood and sprinkled it on the lintel and doorposts (ibid., verse 7).
in haste. Quickly (ibid., verse 11).
